prompt.context: Omega is an aerospace defense contractor with three naval radar systems in its product lineup. These systems are equipped on naval destroyers and aircraft carriers. They have three radar systems: Products 1, 2, and 3. Products 1 and 3 are substitutes for one another. The company has experienced declining profits in recent years and has brought us in to advise how to turn around their financials.
prompt.question: How would you advise Omega Naval Systems to improve its profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Does Omega sell to customers other than the US Navy?
clarifying_info.a: No. They only sell to the US Navy with no intention of expanding to other branches.

clarifying_info.q: Does Omega have ongoing service contracts or recurring revenue?
clarifying_info.a: No. Omega makes money on the sale of the radar system only. It is a one-time sale.
No new products are expected to be developed or launched.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific profitability improvement target?
clarifying_info.a: No target improvement goal — just better than what it currently is.

clarifying_info.q: Are there historic profitability figures available?
clarifying_info.a: No historic profitability figures are available.

clarifying_info.q: Are all three product lines open for discussion, including shutting one down?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. All options are on the table regarding the three product lines.

clarifying_info.q: If one product is shut down, what happens to its customers?
clarifying_info.a: Expect 100% conversion of customers from Product 1 to Product 3, or Product 3 to Product 1, if either is shut down.

exhibits.title: Revenues and Costs by Product
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing costs as a percentage of revenue per unit for Products 1, 2, and 3, broken down by cost category (Fixed Costs, Labor, Semi Conductor Parts*, Software*, Research and Development, Service). Also a table showing year of product launch, units sold in 2017, revenue per unit (millions), and cumulative units sold since launch for each product. Items marked * are externally sourced.

Product_1.note: bars sum to approximately 62% visible; total costs shown as 111% of revenue in answer key

Product_2.note: total costs 79% of revenue per answer key — read absolute bar heights from chart

Product_3.note: total costs 109% of revenue per answer key

exhibits.title: Learning Curve — Total Production Costs vs. Cumulative Units Produced
exhibits.shows: A line chart plotting total production costs (as a percentage, y-axis 0–120%) against cumulative units produced (x-axis 0–180). The curve decreases as cumulative production increases and flattens after a certain volume.

data.pattern: Costs decline as cumulative units double; curve flattens after approximately 80 cumulative units

framework: Profit = Revenue - Costs: diagnose where profitability problem is occurring year-over-year
Revenue drivers: Price per unit, Volume (units sold), Product mix across three product lines, Any service/maintenance revenue (none in this case)
Cost drivers: Labor, Materials (semi-conductor parts, software — both externally sourced), R&D, Service, Fixed overhead/Fixed costs
Market context: Single customer (US Navy), government budget cycles (war-time vs. peace-time demand), political influence on military budgets, potential new deep-tech competitors
Strategic options: Remove a product line, insource vs. outsource components, value-based pricing, digitizing the value chain, expanding capabilities to other industries

questions.prompt: Question 1: Why are there such significant differences in costs as a percentage of revenue across the three products?
questions.guidance:
Product 1 (launched 2017): New product, heavy service costs early in product life cycle. High fixed costs relative to Products 2 and 3 — opportunity to realize economies of scale with volume. Total costs are 111% of revenues (loss-making).
Product 2 (launched 2000): The only profitable product. Highest revenue per unit ($7M). Model for what is working in the company. Total costs are 79% of revenues.
Product 3 (launched 1986): Old product. Heavily outsourced — few suppliers can supply the legacy technology needed, so pricing bargaining power is not in Omega's favor. Total costs are 109% of revenues (loss-making).

questions.prompt: Question 2: Calculate profitability by product line and total current profitability for the firm.
questions.guidance: Multiply profit per unit by units sold (2017) for each product, then sum.

math.setup: Revenue per unit and cost % from Exhibit 1. Total cost per unit = Revenue per unit × (cost % of revenue). Profit per unit = Revenue per unit − Total cost per unit. Total profit = Profit per unit × Units sold.
steps: Product 1: Revenue/unit = $5M; Total cost = 111% × $5M = $5.55M; Profit/unit = $5M − $5.55M = −$0.55M; Units sold = 5; Total profit = −$0.55M × 5 = −$2.75M
Product 2: Revenue/unit = $7M; Total cost = 79% × $7M = $5.53M; Profit/unit = $7M − $5.53M = $1.47M; Units sold = 10; Total profit = $1.47M × 10 = $14.7M
Product 3: Revenue/unit = $5M; Total cost = 109% × $5M = $5.45M; Profit/unit = $5M − $5.45M = −$0.45M; Units sold = 5; Total profit = −$0.45M × 5 = −$2.25M

questions.prompt: Question 3 (conceptual): What would happen if you doubled the sales of Product 1?
questions.guidance: Fixed costs would be shared across more units, lowering the cost per unit. If sales doubled from 5 to 10 units, the fixed cost burden per unit would roughly halve, pushing Product 1 closer to or at breakeven. All else equal, the product line would become profitable (cost drops to approximately 99% of revenue).

math.setup: Conceptual: fixed costs spread over 2× units; variable costs unchanged per unit.
steps: Fixed cost component of Product 1 ≈ 27% of $5M = $1.35M per unit; across 5 units = $6.75M total fixed costs
If units double to 10: fixed cost per unit = $6.75M / 10 = $0.675M, or 13.5% of $5M revenue
New cost % ≈ (111% − 27%) + 13.5% = 84% + 13.5% = 97.5% → approximately 99% of revenue per casebook guidance
math.answer: Doubling Product 1 sales drops its total cost to approximately 99% of revenue, making it profitable.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: Assuming Omega cannot sell more contracts, how would you determine areas for improvement in the cost structure of each product line?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify approaches to cost analysis before Exhibit 2 is revealed. Strong candidates will mention looking at historic cost behavior as the most important inference.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 analysis: What do you observe in the learning curve chart, and what does it mean for each product line?
questions.guidance:
Every time a product doubles its cumulative production after its first 5 units, total production costs are reduced by 20% (learning curve / experience curve effect). The cost reduction persists until 80 units are cumulatively produced, after which no further improvement occurs.
• Product 1 (5 cumulative units): Best opportunity for cost improvement — still at the steep part of the curve. Accelerate production as quickly as possible to achieve profitability sooner.
• Product 2 (185 cumulative units): Has achieved its best cost behavior and peak profitability. It is the cash cow.
• Product 3 (520 cumulative units): Too expensive to continue producing. No more opportunity to reduce cost via the learning curve.

questions.prompt: Given the learning curve insights and the ability to convert 100% of Product 3 customers to Product 1, calculate the profitability improvement from sunsetting Product 3.
questions.guidance: Sunset Product 3 and redirect all 5 of its sales to Product 1. Product 1 now sells 10 units (5 original + 5 converted), doubling cumulative production. Per the learning curve, costs fall 20%: new cost = 111% × 80% = 88.8% of revenue. Recalculate total profit and net margin, then compare to the baseline.

math.setup: New Product 1: 10 units sold; new cost % = 111% × 0.80 = 88.8% of revenue. Product 3 is shut down (0 units, 0 revenue, 0 cost). Product 2 unchanged.
steps: New Product 1: Revenue/unit = $5M; Total cost = 88.8% × $5M = $4.44M; Profit/unit = $5M − $4.44M = $0.56M; Units = 10; Total profit = $0.56M × 10 = $5.6M
Change in net margin = 16.9% − 8.1% = 8.8 percentage points; percentage improvement = ($20.3M − $9.7M) / $9.7M ≈ 109%
math.answer: Profit improves by $10.6M (from $9.7M to $20.3M); net margin improves from 8.1% to 16.9%, a ~109% improvement in net profit.

brainstorming.prompt: Assuming Omega cannot sell more contracts, how would you determine areas for improvement in the cost structure for each product line?

categories.name: Supply Chain
ideas: Conduct supply chain network assessment to identify inefficiencies
Negotiate relationship pricing for externally sourced products (semi-conductor parts, software)
Evaluate number of suppliers for legacy parts in Product 3 and assess bargaining power

categories.name: Labor & Operations
ideas: Compare labor costs to industry averages
Identify historic cost behavior with other Omega product lines (most important inference)
Assess insourcing opportunities for externally sourced components

categories.name: Learning Curve / Experience Effects
ideas: Track historic cost reduction patterns from continuous improvement
Identify economies of scale opportunities as cumulative production increases
Assess software efficiency gains over time

categories.name: Strategic Options
ideas: Value-based pricing given single-customer monopoly relationship
Digitize the value chain to reduce overhead
Explore expanding capabilities or products to other defense branches or industries

recommendation: Shut down Product 3 and redirect all five annual sales to Product 1. Because Products 1 and 3 are substitutes and 100% customer conversion is expected, this doubles Product 1 volume to 10 units per year.

The doubling of Product 1 cumulative production triggers a 20% cost reduction per the learning curve, bringing Product 1's cost to 88.8% of revenue and making it profitable. This improves total firm profit by $10.6M (from $9.7M to $20.3M) and nearly doubles the net margin from 8.1% to 16.9%.
risks: Customer preferences: some Navy customers may prefer Product 3 and resist conversion
Internal pushback: workforce and teams dedicated to Product 3 may face displacement
Shutdown costs: one-time costs to wind down Product 3 production (not yet quantified)
Production capacity: Product 1 manufacturing capacity must be able to absorb 10 units/year
next_steps: Conduct a cost analysis of the Product 3 shutdown (one-time charges, contract close-out obligations)
Develop a communications plan — both internally (workforce) and externally (US Navy customer) — about the proposed transition
Confirm production capacity and lead times for Product 1 can absorb the additional volume
Monitor Product 1 costs as cumulative units increase to validate the learning curve benefit
